Clinical Vignette: Tariq

Tariq is a 27-year-old married physical therapist of Lebanese descent who presents with a quiet, careful manner that takes several sessions to soften into something more candid. He chooses his words deliberately, often pausing mid-sentence as though weighing the cost of each one. He is well-regarded at the rehabilitation clinic where he works, known among colleagues for his patience with difficult cases and his ability to put anxious patients at ease. There is an irony in this that he himself has begun to notice.

Two years ago, Tariq was sexually assaulted by a male acquaintance at a gathering he attended while his wife, Nadia, was visiting family abroad. The assault occurred in a private room after Tariq had been drinking, and he spent the weeks that followed convincing himself it was something other than what it was. He tells himself he is a man. He tells himself men do not experience this. He did not report it, did not tell Nadia, and returned to work the following Monday as though the weekend had been unremarkable.

For the first several months, he functioned through sheer momentum. Then the momentum began to fail him. He started waking between two and four in the morning, heart already loud before his eyes opened, certain that something in the room had shifted. He would lie still for an hour or more, listening. He stopped sleeping on his back entirely because the position triggered a physical response he cannot fully articulate — a tightening across his chest, a sensation of being held down — and so he curls on his side now, close to the edge of the bed, which Nadia has quietly noticed and quietly said nothing about.

His work has become the most complicated terrain. Physical therapy requires sustained, purposeful touch — hands on shoulders, on hips, on the muscles of the lower back — and Tariq is skilled at this. But there are moments, particularly with male patients who are larger than him or who make unexpected movements, when something shifts beneath his professionalism. His jaw tightens. He finds a reason to step back, to adjust equipment, to create distance. He has not hurt anyone. He has not made an error. But he finishes some shifts feeling wrung out in a way that has nothing to do with physical fatigue, and he sits in his car in the parking garage longer than he used to.

He has become someone who scans rooms. He notes exits. At the clinic's holiday party last December, he stood near the door for forty minutes before telling Nadia he had a headache and asking to leave. She believed him, and her believing him made him feel worse.

He describes his relationship with Nadia as loving but increasingly distant, though the distance is something he is constructing from his side of the wall. She reaches for him and he finds ways to redirect — he is tired, he has an early patient, he will be better on the weekend. He loves her without question. The thought of her knowing what happened to him produces a shame so acute he describes it as physical, like something pressing on his sternum.

He carries a particular belief that has settled into him over these two years: that what happened was a failure of his own judgment, his own body, his own masculinity. He has read enough about trauma to know, intellectually, that this is not accurate. Knowing it intellectually has not loosened its grip. He came to therapy not because he believed he deserved help, but because he had begun to notice himself becoming someone he did not recognize — short-tempered, hollowed out, going through the careful motions of a life he feels increasingly outside of.

He is still showing up. To work, to his marriage, to these sessions. He describes this as stubbornness. It may also be something else.
